title: Your kid wants to play Grand Theft Auto VI? Here's what you need to know

blocks.text: Entertainment

The latest Grand Theft Auto instalment continues in the franchise tradition of riling folks up with its mature content, inevitably boosting the game's illicit allure for kids. Experts share tips on navigating its release with young gamers.
Given game's pop culture impact, experts encourage talking to kids about it
Gamer or not, it's nigh impossible to ignore Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest from the uber-successful, controversy-courting video game franchise.

From giant billboards to takeovers of subway stations and sports arenas to the palpable fan excitement, the new instalment has burst into the public consciousness just ahead of North America's holiday season.

It continues the franchise's tradition of riling up folks with its mature content, which inevitably boosts the game's illicit allure — particularly to kids. Experts share what parents should know and tips on navigating the game's release with young gamers.
Adult content, plain and simple
Grand Theft Auto VI revolves around a couple committing crimes. It's made for adults.

The Entertainment Software Rating Board brands it for players 17 or older due to "blood and gore, intense violence, mature humour, nudity, strong language, strong sexual content and use of drugs and alcohol."
GTA VI is an 'astonishing' open world, but no revolution in gaming, says CBC reviewer
Parents should be considering it the same way they'd judge movies or TV shows, says Dr. Tyler Black, a child and adolescent psychiatrist from the University of British Columbia.
"It's going to have explicit drug use. It's going to have real-world crimes… It's definitely the type of game that is well beyond what prepubescent kids should be playing," he said.
At the same time, he said, if you're OK with your teen watching an R-rated movie or a mature-rated series like HBO's Euphoria, you might be OK with them playing GTA VI.

At launch, the game is a solo-player experience. But GTA's incredibly popular online multiplayer format — a shared world where you play alongside friends and strangers — is expected later and is something else for parents to consider, says Jasmine Hood Miller, director of family resources at Common Sense Media, a U.S. non-profit that creates reviews and advice about media and tech in kids' lives.
"In a game that's built for adults, that means that teens can be playing alongside adult strangers with limited moderation or parental visibility," Miller said from Philadelphia.

blocks.text: Parental controls only go so far
Naturally, you don't have to buy the game and can tap parental control settings to block GTA VI from your household's PlayStation or Xbox.

Yet given the wider cultural impact the game is expected to have, Black says these efforts would only amount to a partial restriction. Even without having the game, he noted, kids could encounter GTA VI content at a friend's home, in social media posts or while watching videos from their favourite YouTuber or Twitch streamers.

"Everybody's going to be talking about it. There's going to be a million memes about it. So it's less about does it exist or not in your kid's world and more about how are you going to help them interpret it," he said.
Grand Theft Auto VI-mania hits Canada

Miller also advises parents to talk to their kids: ask what they've seen, heard or feel about the game and, if they're itching to play, explore the whys behind that. She advocates being open about concerns and your family's values during these conversations.
Another tip? Check in with fellow parents about what they're doing, which might potentially address kids' FOMO — fear of missing out — if not allowed to play, she said.
And parents who ultimately decide "no" could soften the blow by framing it as "not yet," she said, and revisit that later.
Research and stay aware

Aside from parents learning more themselves — reading about GTA VI or, if it's appropriate, watching gameplay videos with or even playing alongside their kids — both experts encourage more investment in what kids are seeing and doing online.
"It's just so important for parents to be aware of what kids are watching and consuming," Black said, so as to help them interpret and process what they encounter.

When kids play soccer, he pointed out, parents usually know all about it, from stats and achievements to details about teammates. So give your kids' video game exploits that same attention.
"Parents should know what game [their kids are] playing, how good they are at that game… who do they play with and all those other things," Black said.
"Parents can often do the old 'kid plays the video game by themselves' type of thing, and I wouldn't do that for a game like GTA."
